name: David Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mostly lectures and seminars for law, three days on campus, then two evenings stacking shelves at a warehouse on the ring road. I share a flat with two lads from my course, and we argue about whose turn it is to buy washing-up liquid. My dad drives a city bus and is the union rep at his depot, so I grew up on picket-line sandwiches. The reading is heavy and I'm still working out how to take notes. Honestly I like it, but I keep doing sums about debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: wait and see, and don't believe the salesmen. We've had grand promises before and mostly got worse customer service lines. Online I would probably roll my eyes and post nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm relieved. If AI is a bit of hype, a law degree stays worth something and I can follow my plan. But I know the legal firms are already trying software for contract checking, and I don't trust them to share the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as now. I'd keep the warehouse shifts, about fifteen hours a week, and put aside forty pounds a month towards my second-year rent. I'd join the law society's free mentoring scheme and ask for a vacation placement in the summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, a bit dull, but fine. I'm not frightened. I'm just always a little tight on money, and that doesn't go away because a computer program is overrated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the warehouse. Would AI change anything about that job or about your course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, the warehouse already uses scanners that tell you where to walk, and nobody's asked us about it. Software bosses the shift. I just keep my head down and count the minutes. The course feels safer because nobody here uses AI for anything beyond spell-check, at least as far as I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the money worry, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents cover the rent, and I have about nine hundred in savings from my summer job. Student loan fees on top mean I'll leave owing a lot, and the interest is what scares me. A plateau doesn't fix the debt, but at least a law salary would still be there to pay it off.

say: I'd say **wait and see**, because we've heard big promises before and little changed.
I'd barely post online, and if I did I'd mock the hype.
think: I'm quietly **relieved**, since a law degree should keep its value if little changes.
I still don't trust firms to share any savings with ordinary staff.
do: Keep the **warehouse shifts**, about fifteen hours a week.
Put aside **forty pounds** a month towards second-year rent.
Join the law society mentoring scheme and ask for a summer **placement**.
feel: Steady and a little dull, with a constant **money squeeze** that has nothing to do with AI.
S0.quote: A plateau doesn't fix the debt, but at least a law salary would still be there to pay it off.
fieldNote: Relief is real, but the **debt interest** sits under everything he says.
Distrust of employers is stronger than distrust of the technology itself.
Already lives with warehouse scanners, so he knows software bosses are not hypothetical.

steps.text: Keep the fifteen weekly warehouse shifts through first year
Put forty pounds a month aside for second-year rent
Apply for a summer law placement through the mentoring scheme

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what unions have warned about for years. If AI takes the writing, checking and booking jobs, then companies need to be made to share the gains. I'd say that loudly in the student union and at my dad's depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm scared law is right in the firing line. Junior lawyers do a lot of document checking and drafting, and that's exactly what the software does. I could finish my degree and find the training contracts halved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop being a passive member and actually stand for the student union committee. I'd also attend two union meetings a term with my dad's branch, and ask the careers office hard questions about graduate hiring. Maybe look at moving towards employment law, because that one needs a human at a tribunal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like running up a down escalator. I'm doing everything right and the floor is still moving, and I get angrier at the firms than I'm afraid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the warehouse software bosses the shift. What does that look like if it spreads to office work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the warehouse, scanners already pick the route. If office jobs go the same way, I think about my flatmate Jonas, who's doing the same course. He'd just say we'll use AI to do the work faster. I'd say faster for whom?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say about this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would say organise, don't panic. He lost a route to a timetable app once and the depot fought it for two years. He's proud I'm doing law, but he'd say learn the law that protects people. So I think employment law is where I'm heading.

say: I'd say this is why **unions** matter and companies must share the gains.
I'd say it loudly at the student union and at my dad's depot.
think: Junior lawyers do **document checking**, which is exactly what software takes first.
I could finish my degree and find training contracts **halved**.
do: Stand for the **student union** committee this spring.
Attend two **union meetings** a term with my dad's branch.
Ask careers staff hard questions and lean towards **employment law**.
feel: Like running up a **down escalator**, and angrier at the firms than afraid.
S1.quote: I'm doing everything right and the floor is still moving, and I get angrier at the firms than I'm afraid.
fieldNote: Frames it as **collective** rather than personal, shaped by his father's depot.
Identifies employment law as an answer, which suggests real thought rather than a slogan.
Anger is the main emotion, fear second.

steps.text: Stand for the student union committee in the spring election
Go to two branch union meetings a term with my dad
Ask the careers office how many law firms still hire graduates
Choose employment law options for second year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments are asleep at the wheel and everyone should be in the street. Two years is nothing. Hardly anyone in my seminar has even thought about it, and I'd tell them to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd be sick with worry. By 2028 I'm in my second year, and the jobs I'm studying for might not exist when I finish. Everything my mum and dad saved for me would feel wasted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every protest and every union meeting and push for a basic income and a ban on firing people to swap in AI. I'd also keep the warehouse job, because robots take longer. I'd ask my dad whether the bus depot has any apprenticeships, as a backup. I wouldn't use the AI tools myself. I won't help train my replacement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, if I'm being straight. I'd lie awake doing the sums on debt. It feels like the rug is pulled before I even stood on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, what changes about your degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robots giving me three more years is the one thing I'd hold on to. Warehouse work, bus driving, care work, those would last until about 2031. It's grim that the safe jobs are the ones my family already does, and not the one I'm borrowing money to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does it matter that robots for hands-on work come about three years later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My degree would be half done and worth far less. I'd probably finish it anyway because dropping out looks worse and gets nothing back. But I'd spend my spare time organising rather than studying, because the politics matter more than the grades if the whole system shifts.

say: I'd say governments are **asleep** and that two years is nothing.
I'd tell people in my seminar to start paying attention now.
think: The jobs I'm studying for may **not exist** when I finish.
I fear my parents' help towards my degree would be **wasted**.
do: Join every **protest** and union meeting and push for a basic income.
Keep the **warehouse job**, since robots reach it later.
Ask my dad about **apprenticeships** at the bus depot as a backup.
feel: **Alarmed**, with sleepless nights doing debt sums before I've even started.
S2.quote: The safe jobs are the ones my family already does, and not the one I'm borrowing money to learn.
fieldNote: Refuses to use AI tools on principle, which **limits** his options but not his anger.
Sees robot delay as a thin consolation, noticing the irony for his own family.
Debt is the thread that turns worry into alarm.

steps.text: Join the union-backed protest marches and write to my local MP
Keep the warehouse shifts while robots take longer to arrive
Ask Dad about apprenticeships at the bus depot
Skip AI tools and refuse to help train replacements

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years I'd say is enough time to do something about it politically, if people wake up. I'd say we need retraining funds, shorter work weeks and a tax on the firms that profit. It's a campaign slogan but I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd privately think I could scrape a junior job for two years and then be out on my ear. That's worse in a way, because I'd have debt and no future with the firm. But it gives time to build a different path, so I'm not dead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree with a decent mark, because it's still a good qualification for tribunals and public service. I'd aim at employment law and trade union work, and apply for graduate jobs in advice centres and unions. I'd save a thousand pounds a year from the warehouse for a rainy day. And I'd keep organising with my dad's branch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with something to push against. Five years means I can act, so it's a better kind of fear than the two-year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd have four years of study and then a year or two of work before AGI. How does that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means panic and street politics. Five years means a plan, and a chance to shape what happens instead of being run over. I'd finish the degree, pick the human-facing parts of law and build a safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes between the two-year and five-year versions for your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be sensible and go after jobs where a person in the room matters: tribunals, advice work, union reps. Those might hold on a bit longer. But I won't pretend it's safe. My flatmate Jonas thinks he'll be fine because he's good at computers. I'm less sure anyone will be.

say: I'd say five years is enough to **campaign**, with retraining funds and a tax on firms that profit.
I'd call it a slogan, but I'd mean it.
think: I could **scrape** a junior job for two years and then be out.
At least the time lets me build a **different path**.
do: Finish the degree with a **decent mark** and aim at employment law.
Apply to **advice centres** and unions for graduate roles.
Save **a thousand pounds** a year from warehouse wages.
feel: Anxious, but with something to **push against**, which is better than helpless.
S3.quote: Two years means panic and street politics. Five years means a plan, and a chance to shape what happens instead of being run over.
fieldNote: Time converts his fear into **organising**, a clear difference from the two-year answer.
Picks human-facing law for sensible reasons rather than wishful thinking.
Still doubtful about flatmates who feel safe because they are good with computers.

steps.text: Finish first-year law with a solid mark in every module
Apply to advice centres and unions for graduate roles
Save a thousand pounds a year from warehouse wages
Keep attending union branch meetings with my dad

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years I'd say is a generation of breathing room. We need school and university to change, shorter weeks, and proper public support for people who lose work. I'd say it calmly, because panicking helps no one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, a decade makes my law degree look fine, to be honest. I could get ten years of work, pay off a good chunk of the loan, and maybe move into something else. I'd still worry, but not at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on the law degree, finish, and take the junior job when I can. I'd try to spend about five years in employment law or union work and build savings. I'd put money into a stocks-and-shares account, small, around fifty a month. I'd keep voting and organising throughout, because the decade is only useful if somebody pushes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but proper normal. It's like knowing the weather will turn. I'd have time to find a coat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, does your plan look different from the five-year one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably tell Dad that the depot should push the bus company on retraining before the robots come, since drivers would be hit around 2039. He'd be nearing retirement by then, so he might be safe, but my younger cousins wouldn't be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your dad, if the ten years really are there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say I told you so about unions and then ask whether I'm eating properly. But yes, the plan is law first, then see. A ten-year warning is the best of the three, as long as governments don't waste it the way they always do.

say: I'd say a decade is **breathing room**, but schools and public support need to change.
I'd say it calmly, because panic helps nobody.
think: A decade means my law degree still pays, and I can clear a **chunk of debt**.
I'd still worry, but not at **night**.
do: Finish the degree and take a **junior job** in employment law or union work.
Open a small **shares account** at fifty pounds a month.
Keep voting and **organising** through the whole decade.
feel: Uneasy but **normal**, like knowing the weather will turn and having time to find a coat.
S4.quote: A ten-year warning is the best of the three, as long as governments don't waste it the way they always do.
fieldNote: Ten years softens everything, but his distrust of **governments** stays.
Shows concern for his father's depot and younger cousins, not only himself.
Plans are modest and sensible, close to what a normal law graduate would do.

steps.text: Finish the law degree and apply for junior employment law roles
Open a small shares account with fifty pounds a month
Keep voting and helping at union campaigns each year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most. I'd be mid-degree, in debt, with nothing finished and no time to change course. What would help is real public support: retraining that pays you a wage, a basic income, and rules that make firms share the gains. Without that, ordinary people carry all the risk.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that people think students like me are naive. We're not. We see debt, rent and warehouse scanners every week. We know the sums. We just want a fair deal rather than a sermon about adapting.

headlineQuote: We see debt, rent and warehouse scanners every week. We know the sums. We just want a fair deal rather than a sermon about adapting.
portrait: **David Alvarez** is 18, a first-year law student, sharing a flat and working fifteen warehouse hours a week.
His dad is a bus driver and union rep, so he reaches for **collective action** and unions first.
He never uses AI tools and distrusts employers more than the technology.
He moves from uneasy in a plateau to **alarmed** if AGI arrives in 2028, with debt as the thread.
More time calms him, and he heads towards employment law, where a person in the room still matters.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI scenario worries him most, mid-degree, in debt and with no time to change course.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **retraining on a wage**, a basic income and rules that make firms share the gains.
